t: LeetCode 2386 — Find the K-Sum of an Array
o: We must find the k-th largest subsequence sum, counting duplicates. The largest possible sum is simply the sum of all positive elements (take every positive, drop every negative). Every other subsequence sum equals this maximum minus the sum of some subset of absolute values |nums[i]| — because excluding a positive p reduces the sum by p, while including a negative v reduces it by |v|. So the problem becomes: given the array of absolute values, find the k-th largest value obtainable by subtracting a subset-sum of absolute values from the maximum. Since k <= 2000, we never need more than k states, which makes a best-first search with a max-heap feasible even though there are 2^n subsets.
k: The maximum subsequence sum is the sum of all positive elements; any subsequence sum equals that maximum minus a subset-sum of the absolute values.
Reframe the problem as finding the k largest 'deficits' (subset sums of absolute values), then answer = maxSum - kthLargestDeficit.
A max-heap best-first search over (index, deficit) states visits only O(k log k) states instead of enumerating all 2^n subsets.

a.n: Approach 1: Best-first search with a visited set
a.i: Sort absolute values in decreasing order. Start from the maximum sum with index 0 (nothing excluded yet). From state (index i, current sum s) we may either keep s and move to i+1 (skip |a[i]|), or move to s - a[i] at i+1 (exclude it). Because the array is sorted descending, popping the largest sum first guarantees each pop yields the next-largest achievable sum, exactly like Dijkstra/best-first search. A visited set prevents processing the same (index, sum) twice.
s: Compute base = sum of all positive elements; build array a of absolute values sorted descending.
Push (-base, 0) into a min-heap keyed by negated sum; mark (0, base) visited.
Pop k-1 times; for each popped (negS, i) with i < n, push (negS + a[i], i+1) (exclude a[i]) and (negS, i+1) (skip), marking visited.
The k-th popped sum is the answer.
a.t: O(k log k + n log n) — sorting dominates, and the loop performs O(k) heap operations each O(log k).
a.sp: O(n + k) — the sorted array plus heap and visited set holding at most O(k) states.

a.n: Approach 2: Heap without a visited set (parent-pointer trick)
a.i: Duplicates in Approach 1 come from reaching the same exclusion set via different paths. We can eliminate them structurally: define a state (i, s) where s excludes a subset of a[0..i-1] that includes a[i-1]'s decision chain implicitly. From (i, s) push (s - a[i+1], i+1) — additionally exclude a[i+1] — and (s + a[i] - a[i+1], i+1) — drop a[i] from the excluded set and exclude a[i+1] instead. This generates each subset exactly once (standard technique for k-th subset sums), so no visited set is needed.
s: Sort absolute values descending; compute base = sum of positives.
If n == 1, answer directly: k == 1 ? max(nums[0], 0) : 0.
Seed the heap with (base - a[0], 0); pop k-1 times.
For popped (s, i): push (s - a[i+1], i+1); if i > 0 also push (s + a[i] - a[i+1], i+1).
Add the last popped value to base and return it.

c.python:
import heapq
class Solution:
    def kSum(self, nums: List[int], k: int) -> int:
        n = len(nums)
        if n == 1:
            return max(nums[0], 0) if k == 1 else 0
        a = sorted((abs(x) for x in nums), reverse=True)
        base = sum(x for x in nums if x > 0)
        heap = [(a[0], 0)]
        val = 0
        for _ in range(k - 1):
            d, i = heapq.heappop(heap)
            val = d
            heapq.heappush(heap, (d + a[i + 1], i + 1))
            if i > 0:
                heapq.heappush(heap, (d - a[i] + a[i + 1], i + 1))
        return base - val

a.t: O(n log n + k log k) — sorting plus k heap operations of size O(k).
a.sp: O(n + k) — sorted array and heap; no visited set needed.

w: In an interview, present Approach 1 first (it is easier to reason about correctness via best-first search) and mention Approach 2 as an optimization removing the visited set. Key pitfalls: (1) forgetting that negatives contribute via their absolute values — the base sum uses only positives; (2) overflow — sums reach 10^5 * 10^9 = 10^14, so use 64-bit integers in C++/Java and plain numbers in JS (safe here since 10^14 < 2^53); (3) the empty subsequence means 0 is always available, handled automatically since deficits only grow; (4) the n == 1 edge case in Approach 2's seeding. Likely follow-ups: return all top-k sums as a list, or handle streaming updates to nums.
